name: Victor Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's my aunt Marta's farm, a bit of everything: 80 ewes, a dozen beef cattle, a field of potatoes, some veg, laying hens, and a farm shop out on the main road. Weekdays I'm in the yard from seven, feeding, mucking out, fixing whatever's broken, which is usually the fence the ewes have pushed over. Weekends I'm mostly behind the till in the shop, selling lamb, eggs, potatoes and Marta's cakes. I'm still learning the farming side, Marta's patient but she does sigh a lot.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Which part do you like more, the yard or the shop?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The shop, if I'm honest, which surprises people. I like the regulars, old Mr Ochieng who buys six eggs and talks for twenty minutes, the families on a Saturday. I use one of those AI chat apps now and then to write the posts for the shop's page and the price signs, it saves me an hour. What wears me out is lambing, I'm not a natural at it, and Marta's knees aren't what they were, so it falls on me more each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That'd suit us fine. Small farms like ours don't have money for robots anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news for places like ours, because the big farms don't get to race ahead with machines we can't afford. I'd probably joke about it in the shop, something like, at least the robots won't be selling cakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be pleased but not too pleased. Nothing changing also means the shop's takings stay flat and Marta still can't afford a second full-timer. So I'm still doing lambing alone on two hours' sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, and push a veg box scheme we've talked about, delivering to the new houses on the edge of town on Thursdays. I'd keep using the chat app for posts and maybe for working out the box prices. And keep putting by, I've got about four months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would buy the veg boxes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Young families in the new estate, the ones who drive past the shop but never stop. People like the idea of a farm more than they like stopping at one. A box on the doorstep is the farm coming to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there talk of you taking the farm on from Marta someday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's talk. She's got no kids and she's 63. I've not said yes yet, because I'm not sure I'm good enough, and I'm not sure it can pay two of us, let alone just me with a mortgage.

S0.say: I'd say it's good news for small farms, because the big ones can't race ahead with machines we can't afford. I'd joke in the shop that at least robots won't be selling cakes.
S0.think: I'd be pleased but not too pleased, because nothing changing means flat takings and no money for a second full-timer. I'd still be lambing alone on little sleep.
S0.do: Carries on at his aunt's farm and launches a Thursday veg box delivery to a new housing estate. Uses the chat app for posts and box pricing, and keeps adding to about four months of savings.
S0.quote: People like the idea of a farm more than they like stopping at one. A box on the doorstep is the farm coming to them.
S0.fieldNote: Victor sees the plateau as protection for small farms against richer, more automated neighbours. His real question is whether to take over the farm from his aunt, which runs under everything. He's more confident in the shop than in the yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels likely, and honestly mixed for us. Some of it could help, some of it could hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say use the good bits and keep the human bits. A farm shop works because people like talking to someone who knows where the lamb came from. I'd say that to customers, and I'd probably put it on the shop's page too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the yard work is the bit that's at risk, which is the bit I'm worst at anyway. If a robot can muck out and check the ewes, that frees me for the shop. But it also means Marta might not need me in the yard, and the shop alone doesn't pay a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good with the AI tools for the shop, ordering, online sales, maybe an egg vending machine by the gate for when we're shut. I'd wait for the yard robots to come down in price and see how they work on other small farms before we bought one. And I'd do a short course on running a small shop, the council runs one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but okay. More curious than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An egg vending machine is a kind of automation too. Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, fair. No, because it's selling Marta's eggs at midnight when nobody would be there anyway. I'm happy for a machine to sell eggs at midnight. I'm not happy for it to sell them at noon to Mr Ochieng.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Marta say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say 'we'll see' and then not do it for a year, then do it all at once. She's careful with money, which is why the farm's still here. I'd have to show her figures from another farm before she'd budge.

S1.say: I'd say use the good bits and keep the human bits, because people buy from a farm shop to talk to someone who knows where the lamb came from. I'd say it to customers and on the shop's page.
S1.think: The yard work is most at risk, and that's the bit I'm worst at, so robots could free me for the shop. But the shop alone doesn't pay a wage.
S1.do: Gets good with AI tools for ordering and online sales and puts an egg vending machine by the gate for after hours. Waits to see yard robots work on other small farms before buying, and takes a council course on running a small shop.
S1.feel: Uneasy but okay, more curious than worried.
S1.quote: I'm happy for a machine to sell eggs at midnight. I'm not happy for it to sell them at noon to Mr Ochieng.
S1.fieldNote: Victor draws his line between automating what happens when nobody's there and replacing the conversation at the till. He'd adopt shop tools quickly but wait for proof on yard robots, a steady pattern. His aunt's caution with money shapes his timing as much as his own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Then the big farms are fully robotic and their food gets very cheap, very fast. I don't know how we compete with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say buy local, keep your farm shops open, because once they shut they don't come back. I'd be saying it to every customer. Whether they'd listen when their own jobs were going, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the shop might be the last bit standing, people paying for a human face. But only if people still have money. If the families on the estate lose their jobs, they're not paying extra for our lamb, they're buying robot lamb at half the price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut back hard, me and the farm both. Hold off on any decision about taking over the farm, I wouldn't say yes in a two-year world. Turn the shop more into a café, coffee and cake and a chat, the bit a robot can't really sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A bit like when the river flooded the bottom field and you could only watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a robot can't sell the chat. Are you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not really. Maybe people will want to talk to the robot. I just hope Mr Ochieng won't. Honestly, I don't know what people will want in two years, nobody does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Marta say to each other that week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd make tea and say her father got through the foot-and-mouth outbreak, so we'd get through this. I'd nod and not believe her. Then we'd do the accounts on the kitchen table, like we always do.

S2.say: I'd tell every customer to buy local and keep farm shops open, because once they shut they don't come back. I don't know if they'd listen with their own jobs going.
S2.think: The shop might be the last bit standing, with people paying for a human face, but only if they still have money. If customers lose their jobs, they'll buy cheap robot-farmed lamb instead.
S2.do: Cuts back hard at home and on the farm and holds off on any decision to take over the farm. Turns the shop more toward a café selling coffee, cake and conversation.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like watching a flood cover the bottom field.
S2.quote: Maybe people will want to talk to the robot. I just hope Mr Ochieng won't.
S2.fieldNote: Victor saw quickly that his best hope, the human-facing shop, depends on customers still having wages. He admitted he isn't sure people will prefer a human. The fast timeline would make him put off taking over the family farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives us room to steer, I think. Not much, but some.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small farms should team up, share kit, sell together, before the big ones swallow everything. I'd go to the local farmers' group and actually say it, which I don't usually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think the farm has to become something else to survive. Less food production, more people coming to us: school visits, the café, maybe a few cabins. Robots can grow potatoes, but they can't be a day out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sit down with Marta and plan it out, and do a course on running a rural business. I'd put some of my savings into the café side, new coffee machine, a few tables. And I'd try the robot mucking-out machine once two or three farms near us had one and liked it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a project. Projects help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take the farm on in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If the plan works in the first two years, yes. Five years is enough to try something and see if it breathes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots can't be a day out. What if they can?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we're a day out with a robot in it, I suppose. People will still want to touch a lamb. I'd bet a bit of my savings on that, not all of it.

S3.say: I'd say small farms should team up to share kit and sell together before the big ones swallow everything. I'd actually stand up at the local farmers' group and say it.
S3.think: The farm would have to become a place people visit rather than mainly a food producer, with school visits, a café and maybe cabins. Robots can grow potatoes but can't be a day out.
S3.do: Plans the farm's future with his aunt and takes a rural business course in the first year. Puts some savings into the café side and tries a mucking-out robot once nearby farms have tested it.
S3.feel: Anxious but steadied by having a project.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to try something and see if it breathes.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Victor enough time to test a new direction for the farm before committing to take it over. He'd bet part, not all, of his savings on people wanting a farm day out. He'd speak at the farmers' group, which he says he usually doesn't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That changes the big question for me, about taking the farm on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decade to get ready, and small places like ours should start now: the shop, the café, the visits. And I'd say government should help small farms change, not just the big ones that can afford lawyers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, with ten years I'd say yes to Marta. I'd have time to learn the farm properly while she's still here, bring robots in for the heavy yard work, and build the shop and visitor side. I'd be 37 when it all arrives, running a place that people come to, not a place that just grows things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tell Marta yes, and start the handover slowly. Spend the first few years learning lambing and the books from her, then buy the yard robots once they're cheap and proven. Grow the veg boxes and the café, and keep a year's savings separate from the farm's money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but hopeful. It almost feels like a plan for a life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So more time pushes you toward taking the farm. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd have time to get good at it before I'm on my own. With two years I'd say no to the farm. With ten I'd say yes. It's the same farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Marta say if you told her yes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd cry and then tell me I'm still doing lambing wrong. Then she'd start writing down everything in a notebook, she's been threatening to for years.

S4.say: I'd say it's a decade to get ready, and small farms should start now with shops, cafés and visits. Government should help small farms change, not just the big ones with lawyers.
S4.think: With ten years I'd say yes to taking over the farm, learn it properly while my aunt is still here, and bring in robots for heavy yard work. I'd be 37 running a place people visit, not just a place that grows things.
S4.do: Agrees to take over his aunt's farm and starts a slow handover, learning lambing and the accounts from her. Buys yard robots once they're cheap and proven, grows the veg boxes and café, and keeps a year's savings apart from the farm's money.
S4.feel: Uneasy but hopeful, almost like a plan for a life.
S4.quote: With two years I'd say no to the farm. With ten I'd say yes. It's the same farm.
S4.fieldNote: The amount of warning time flips Victor's biggest life decision: no to the farm at two years, maybe at five, yes at ten. He'd use robots for the heavy work and keep people at the centre of the business. His aunt's knowledge passing to him is a theme that only appears when there's time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there'd be no time to turn the farm into anything else, and our customers would lose their wages at the same moment we needed them most. What would help is grants for small farms to change direction, and some kind of income support so people can still afford to shop somewhere that isn't the cheapest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked about older people like Marta. She's 63, she's put her whole life into this place, and nobody's going to retrain her. If the farm goes, it's not just a job she loses, it's her whole week.

headlineQuote: With two years I'd say no to the farm. With ten I'd say yes. It's the same farm.
portrait: Victor is a 27-year-old junior on his aunt's mixed farm, splitting his week between the yard, where he's still learning, and the farm shop till, where he's at his best. He's a pragmatic centrist who uses AI now and then for the shop's posts and prices. His biggest open question is whether to take over the farm from his aunt, who's 63. The amount of warning time changes that answer: he'd say no with two years, maybe with five, and yes with ten, using robots for the heavy yard work and turning the farm into a place people visit. He fears that fast change would take his customers' wages just when the shop needs them most.
biggestWorry: AGI within two years, because there'd be no time to reshape the farm and customers would lose their wages just when the shop needed them.
whatWouldHelp: Grants for small farms to change direction, and income support so people can still afford to shop somewhere other than the cheapest place.
